This composer wrote 12 piano pieces titled The Seasons as well as an unnumbered symphony named Manfred. Two of his symphonies are titled Winter Daydreams and Polish, and he wrote some other orchestral works such as Serenade for Strings and Romeo and Juliet Fantasy Overture. His sixth symphony has a second movement in five-four time, and canons are called for at the ending of another piece. Identify this composer of Symphony Pathetique [pah-teh-TEEK] and the 1812 Overture.

This artist used a butterfly monogram and, like Gustav Courbet, painted his mistress, Joanna Hiffernan, in front of some abstract trees in Symphony in White, No. 1: The White Girl. This artist painted several works for Frederick Leyland, including designing a room in the Japanese style, The Peacock Room, and sued Jonathan Ruskin over criticism over a work depicting fireworks in London, Nocturne in Black and Gold - The Falling Rocket. Name this artist of a picture of his mother sitting with a white bonnet, Arrangement in Grey and Black.

He criticized Daniel Burnham for that man's classicism and designed the modernist Transportation Building for the Columbian Exposition. His other buildings in Chicago include the Carson Pirie Scott department store and the Auditorium Building for Roosevelt University, and he worked with Dankmer Adler on his most famous project, a red, ten-story skyscraper in St. Louis. Coining the phrase "form follows function," identify this American architect, mentor to Frank Lloyd Wright and designer of the Wainwright building, the father of skyscrapers.

This composer wrote some operas inspired by Hindu myths such as Sita and Savitri. He wrote two suites for military band, a St. Paul's Suite, and A Moorside Suite. He set the poem "I Vow to Thee, My Country" to music in the 4th movement of his most famous piece, the last movement of which is subtitled "the Mystic" and ends with a fadeout effect, and the first movement has a distinctive militaristic theme. Identify this British composer who wrote about the "Bringer of Jollity" and "Bringer of Old Age" in his suite The Planets.

This architect designed a villa for Fritz Tugendhat and his wife, and his Lake Shore Drive Apartments exemplified his "skin and bones" architecture. He also designed the Barcelona chair and table for the German Pavilion, as well as an all steel and glass house for Dr. Farnsworth outside of Chicago. This architect's best known building features the Four Seasons Restaurant and is located on Park Avenue in Manhattan. Associated with the aphorisms "less is more," identify this architect who designed the Seagram building with Philip Johnson.

This composer wrote 10 pieces for piano four hands called The Legends, and earlier he wrote a cycle of 23 pieces for two voices with piano titled Moravian Duets. He wrote a "Nature, Life and Love" trilogy of overtures that includes In Nature's Realm, Carnival, and Othello, and he composed the String Quartet No. 12, nicknamed American, after his time spent in Iowa. His opus 46 and 72 combine to form a series of 16 Slavonic Dances, and his most famous symphony was once mistaken to be his 5th. Identify this Czech composer of the New World Symphony.

This composer wrote a set of 12 violin concertos titled La stravaganza, and he composed another set of 12 concertos for various combinations in L'estro Armonico. He wrote an opera based on "Orlando furioso", and he also composed a Mandolin Concerto in C Major. His most famous collection describes a barking dog, an icy wind, and drunkards, which all appear in his The Contest Between Harmony and Invention. Identify this Baroque composer who included "La Primavera" in his The Four Seasons.

One painting by this man depicts a waiter dressed in white who stands next to a pool table in the title establishment. Another of his paintings shows a peasant family of five sitting underneath a dimly lit lamp while consuming the title food. In addition to The Night Café and The Potato Eaters, this artist set many of his paintings in the city of Arles, and he also executed two portraits of his doctor, Paul Gachet. Name this late 19th century Dutch artist of The Starry Night who painted several self-portraits after cutting off his own ear.

A visit to Munich caused him to be influenced by the Neue Sachlichkeit, or the New Objectivity or Sobriety Movement, as evidenced by the often dour faces in such works as 1929's Woman with Plants. An image of George Washington and a mangled cherry tree is found in Parson Weems' Fable, and his work Arbor Day is on the reverse of the Iowa State Quarter. His sister Nan and his dentist were the models of his most famous work, featuring a stern-faced couple standing in front of a farmouse. FTP name this painter of American Gothic.

The most prominent member of the Young British Artists that emerged in the late 1980s, many of his best-known works are owned by Charles Saatchi. Famous for works made with unconventional materials such a butterfly wings and pill bottles. More famous are sculptures made of animal carcasses preserved in formaldehyde, such as 1991s "The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living" which is a large tiger shark. FTP, identify this artist who made headlines for the $100 sale of a diamond encrusted skull.

W. H. Auden's poem dedicated to John F. Kennedy was the basis for this composer's vocal piece titled Elegy for J.F.K. Robert Woods Bliss commissioned his Concerto in E-flat or "Dumbarton Oaks" Concerto, while Auden was also a collaborator on the libretto for this composer's opera The Rake's Progress. His better known works include a ballet which opens at the Shrovetide Fair and another whose sections include "Adoration of the Earth" and "The Sacrifice." FTP, name this Russian composer of Petrushka, The Firebird, and The Rite of Spring.

This work, its composer's Opus 125, is an appropriate ‘introduction' to the Romantic period of music in the years after it was first performed. Adopted as Europe's anthem by the Council of Europe in 1972, the most famous section, from the 4th Movement, is instantly recognizable to non-music lovers and was quoted by Brahms in his 1st Symphony. The first major orchestral work to feature a prominent and demanding choral section, it was ironically composed when its composer's deafness was at its peak. FTP, name this last symphony of Beethoven, featuring the Ode to Joy, nicknamed the Choral Symphony.

Bela Bartok wrote a piece with the name of this genre for Orchestra, which many hold to be his closest attempt at writing a 'full' symphony. Developing from the work of Arcangelo Corelli and Antonio Vivaldi in the late 17th and early 18th century, the work of Bach's sons, especially CPE Bach, was critical in transforming this genre into its modern form. Mozart wrote a total of 4 pieces of this genre for the horn, whilst Richard Strauss produced one for oboe, and Ralph Vaughn Williams, one for the tuba. FTP, name this genre of music which features prominently a solo instrument against an orchestra, famous examples of which include Rachmaninoff's 2nd and 3rd ones for the piano.

Born in 1912 in Cody, Wyoming, he studied under Thomas Hart Benton when he moved to New York, though the influence is not clear in his most famous works. His wife Lee Krasner was also an abstract painter. Famous works include "Autumn Rhythm" at the Metropolitan Museum, and "Full Fathom Five" in which he has embedded buttons, tacks, coins, and cigarette butts. FTP, these are the works of what famous American drip painter?

He began his career by working with such jazz legends as Dizzy Gillespie, Miles Davis, and Thelonius Monk, but introduced his own style in his 1959 album Giant Steps. Strongly inspired by religious mysticism due to his Muslim wife Naima, his music incorporates Sufi, Hindu, and Buddhist themes. FTP, name the celebrated jazz saxophonist who developed his "sheets of sound" music in his 1960 album My Favorite Things as well as his 1964 master work, A Love Supreme.

His life was fictionalized by Alexander Pushkin and turned into an opera by Modest Mussorgsky, and his ascension to the throne marked the end of the Rukrid line of tsars. Although initially popular his line did not survive, and his son faced a series of pretenders and was eventually deposed. FTP name this father of the "true" Dmitry, first tsar of the house of Godunov.

Born on October 27, 1858, he had this presidential portrait painted by John Singer Sargent. To compensate for poor health as a child, as an adult, he adopted a rigorous training schedule. Coming from a long line of Harvard graduates, many progressive reforms were undertaken during his presidency, including improvements in conservation, child labor laws, and food safety. FTP, name the third face from the left on Mount Rushmore, whose sculpture lies between Jefferson and Lincoln.

Beginning with just strings and clarinets, in the recapitulation of the first movement, the bassoons play the same motif as the horns did in the exposition. The last movement features a contrabassoon and a piccolo, the first time it appears in a Beethoven symphony. Premiering after his Sixth Symphony on December 22, 1808, this is FTP, which Beethoven Symphony, often considered the greatest symphony of all time?

Premiering in 1962, a common mistake when writing this character's name is to forget the punctuation mark separating the second and third syllables of his name. Many of this hero's enemies wear green, but he is usually wears blue and red. Other costumes have been metallic version, as well as a famous black one. Name this character, who has recently been publicly unmasked to be a New Yorker named Peter Parker.

This German Romantic composer composed the theme for the 1936 Berlin Olympics, and became President of the Reich Music Bureau, even though his daughter-in-law was Jewish. Married to a soprano, he wrote many operas, most importantly "Elektra" and "Salome." He is also famous for his tone poems including Don Quixote. FTP name this composer whose Also Spracht Zarathustra is used in Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.

A story in Boccaccio's Decameron involves his finding it funny that he was so covered in mud that nobody would recognize him. He designed the freestanding campanile of Florence's Duomo, and one of his earliest paintings was a large crucifix in Santa Maria Novella. Legend has it that he was a shepherd boy discovered by Cimabue while drawing some sheep on some rocks. His masterwork is usually considered to be the fresco cycles in the Scrovegni, or Arena Chapel in Padua. He may also have painted the frescoes in the Basilica of St. Francis in Assisi depicting that saint's life. FTP, name this early 14th-century Italian artist, sometimes considered the first painter of the Renaissance.

In its early phases, this group was influenced by the aesthetic ideas of Johannes Itten, who taught the preliminary course Vorkurs. Three years later, Itten was replaced by the Hungarian designer Laszlo Moholy-Nagy, who rewrote the Vorkurs with an emphasis on New Objectivity. Members of this school include Bruno Taut, Hans Poelzig, and Ernst May, who are credited with thousands of socially progressive housing units built in Dresden, Frankfurt and Berlin. Founded in 1919 by Walter Gropius, FTP, identify this German school of art and architecture that translates to "Building School."

The lighting of this work is a trademark of the artist, as its flow from left to right illuminates the face of the subject. It depicts a bust-length image of the titular figure's dark yellow outergarment. The subject gazes longingly at the viewer while wearing a blue and yellow turban-like headdress. The slight turn of her head allows the main object of the work to hang above her left shoulder. FTP, name this Jan Vermeer painting, turned into a Scarlet Johannson movie about a piece of jewelry,

A form of dance with 'English' and 'Finnish' variations, it was orchestrated into mainstream classical music largely thanks to the efforts of Astor Piazzolla. It is frequently danced either chest to chest or at arms length, and involves syncopated rhythmic footwork. Frequently thought of as an Argentinean dance, it was also developed in neighboring Uruguay. FTP, name this exciting and flamboyant dance form in 3, one of the most popular of ballroom dances

A small jeweled clip holds up part of the subject's hair, which may have been colored with henna. The redness of the subject's right ear in comparison to her skin complexion indicates the use of makeup. Her right hand clutches a small table in the left foreground, while her right shoulder strap was repainted to hang high on her shoulder instead of falling down. FTP, name this scandalous painting of a young socialite in a black dress by John Singer Sargent.

His wife Lee Krasner was an abstract painter, and he was born in 1912 in Cody, Wyoming. Studying under Thomas Hart Benton after moving to New York, though the influence is not clear in his most famous works. Famous works include "Autumn Rhythm" at the Metropolitan Museum, and "Full Fathom Five" in which he has embedded buttons, tacks, coins, and cigarette butts. FTP, these are the works of what famous American drip painter?

Vowing at the age of twelve never to marry, she had illegitimate children with stage designer Gordon Craig and the heir to the Singer sewing machine fortune. She caused controversy by using Beethoven's music, setting one of her most noted works to the Ninth Symphony. A vision of the death of her children inspired another of her works, and several days after the premiere of that, the children drowned in the Seine. She likewise met a tragic end in France when, in Nice, her veil caught in the wheel of her automobile. Name this proponent of Greek revival and modern expressionist dance.

In the center of this painting, a redheaded woman in a brownish-black dress sits in a wooden chair with her back turned, most likely engaged in conversation with the four others at her table. Another redheaded woman wearing pale greenish makeup stares directly at the viewer on the right side. Walking in background past a woman in black adjusting her hair is the artist himself, a small bearded man in a top hat, scoping out the evening crowd at the title location. Name this painting set in a Paris nightclub, a work of Henri Toulouse-Lautrec.

A small bridge spanning the central brook in this painting separates the white buildings in the distant background from the stone ruins and the vast shrubbery that form the backdrop of the foreground scene. The only people depicted are a soldier in red, calmly holding a staff on the left side, and a half-nude woman in white on the right, nursing her baby on the riverbank. Thunder flashes in the sky of what Giorgione painting, whose title refers to the background's brewing storm?

Its contents were collected under oath by agents known as "legati" and it is composed of answers to a series of questions known as the Inquistio Elienis. Although it is still occasionally consulted to settle disputes involving genealogy, the original is usually passed over in favor of reprinted versions like the Victoria County Histories. This work attempted to ascertain the size, resources, and ownership of every plot of land belonging to the newly Norman nation. Identify this product of a 1086 survey that helped William the Conqueror take stock of his kingdom.

Its three styles are jondo, intermedio, and chico. The "alboreás" form is seen at weddings, while the "martinetes" incorporates a hammer and anvil. Using the "palo seco," a stick used to create a rhythm on the floor, it includes the interpretive footwork known as "zapateado," the solo passages called "solea," and the transcendent state of "duende." name this style of dance that sometimes blends with fandango, originating in India and brought to Spain by migrating Roma.

In 1930, a sound remake of this film entitled The Twelfth Hour was made using one of the five known prints of the original to escape destruction. Remade in 1979 by Werner Herzong with Klaus Kinski in the title role, its original had bankrupted the Prana-Film GmbH studio. To avoid copyright problems with the book it unauthorizedly adapted, names and locations were changed such that Max Shreck played Graf Orlock, made up to look like a giant rat rather than a suave Transylvanian nobleman. Name this silent horror masterpiece directed by F.W. Murnau, the first film based on Dracula.

A small patch of white flowers in the lower left foreground provides a contrast to the dismal background and may represent the purity of the title character. Just above the flowers, a child, most likely John the Baptist, kneels in a praying position and holds a thin, elongated cross between his arms. On the right, the angel Uriel sits with the baby Jesus, while the title character sits in the center in a brilliant blue and gold dress that blends seamlessly into the darkness of the background through the artist's use of his trademark sfumato. Name this Leonardo da Vinci painting of Mary in a stone-filled cave.

Three shadowy stone arches form the backdrop of this painting, with light falling on two women sitting on the right: one in a plain white shawl and the other in red, blue and gold, both facing each other and weeping. A third woman behind them in the shadows cries and hunches over two small children. The main action shows a man in red holding out three swords as a trio of soldiers reaches out towards them. Identify this Jacques-Louis David work depicting the titular brothers swearing allegiance to Rome.

Among the building projects undertaken by this monarch were two enormous obelisks, then the largest in the world and still standing in the Red Chamber at Karnak. Ruling under the regnal name Maatkare and clearly attempting to emulate the earlier Sobekneferu, this monarch also sent an expedition to Punt. While archaeologists have recently begun to believe that the erasing of names long blamed on the next ruler actually came much later, someone was clearly offended by such actions as this ruler's assumption of the title "Pharoah" and the wearing of the ceremonial false beard. For 10 points name this successor of Thutmose I, the most powerful woman to rule Egypt before Cleopatra.

Early works by this composer include "Tahiti Trot," "Three Fantastic Dances," and "Aphorisms." He incorporated patriotic texts into his second and third symphonies, subtitled "To October" and "The First of May." His works for the stage include "Hypothetically Murdered," "The Human Comedy," and "The Nose." His symphonies included one inspired by the siege of Leningrad and one labeled "a Soviet artist's reply to just criticism. Name this composer of Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District.

His cousin Nachod, a performing tenor, debuted the role of Waldemar in his song cycle Gurrelieder. His other works include two chamber symphonies, the abstract Music for a Film Scene, and The Book of the Hanging Gardens. He died before finishing the opera Moses und Aron, but he did popularize such concepts as serialism and Sprechstimme as the teacher of Anton Webern. Name this composer of Pierrot Lunaire and Transfigured night.

Every day for a month, this painter went to the Pierre Loeb galley and added to one of his canvases, which by the end of the month portrayed a crust of bread, an apple with a fork in it, and a bottle of gin wrapped in newspaper. In 1967, he collaborated with José Llorens Artigas to create Wall of the Sun and Wall of the Moon, two murals for the Paris UNESCO office, which later commissioned him to design the Picasso Medal. Name this surrealist painter of The Reaper and the afore-described Still Life With Old Shoe, which recorded his feelings upon leaving his Catalan homeland.

Operas by Franz Josef Haydn and Antonio Vivaldi show this character imprisoned in cave by the sorceress Alcina and emerging to discover that Medoro has married his love object Angelica, causing him to go mad briefly. The work that storyline is derived from follows an unfinished epic by Matteo Boiardo, and was itself written by Ludovico Ariosto. In his most notable epic, he is betrayed by his stepfather Ganelon, and dies blowing his horn Olifant to summon troops, but only after using his sword Durendal to make a failed stand against the Saracens that vastly outnumber his men. Name this paladin of Charlemagne and subject of a namesake chansons de geste "song."

According to its score, a baritone can be substituted "if necessary" for the contralto soloist specified in the even-numbered movements of this work, which was conceived when its composer came across a Hans Bethge volume after being diagnosed with valvular malformation. Its sixth and final movement, "Farewell," is as long as the five that precede it. It starts off with a "Drinking Song of Misery," and includes movements entitled "On Youth" and "On Beauty." identify this setting of four eighth-century Chinese poets by Gustav Mahler, concerned with the natural world and the "circle of life."

In The Bride of Frankenstein, Elsa Lancaster's movements were inspired by the stylish motions seen in this film. Rudolf Kleine-Rogge plays the evil scientist Rotwang, who creates Maschinen-Mensch. That is a duplicate of the virtuous Maria. Who has ensnared the affections of John Frederson's son. Briggite Helm plays the robot below the pleasure city of Art Deco buildings and flying cars in, what 1927 film by Fritz Lang?

His first major work was a treatise on rhetoric called the Dialogus. He also produced a detailed study of Germanic peoples and received much correspondence from his contemporary, Pliny the Younger. Heavily critical of Domitian in his biography of his own father-in-law, Agricola, he focused on the rule of the Julio-Claudians like Tiberius and Nero in another historical volume. Name this Roman historian and author of the Annals.

The artist of this painting also created a preceding work showing a mob attacking Mamaluke soldiers on horseback. The action takes place at the hill of Principe Pio, where a man in yellow pants and a white shirt stands amidst a crowd of scared civilians and raises his arms in a Christ-like pose. The bodies and the pool of blood below hint at his fate as a row of soldiers on the right lines up their guns and prepares to fire into the crowd in, what Francisco Goya work depicting the executions of the titular day?

One collection by this name is housed in the Pallazzo Venier dei Leoni in Venice. Its newest branch opened in Las Vegas's Venetian resort in 2001, while the original was contracted by Hilla Rebay as the Museum of Non-Objective Painting. The inverted ziggurat and the winding spiral connecting the galleries were designed by Frank Lloyd Wright. Name these museums, whose flagship branch houses the world's largest Kandinsky collection, in Manhattan.

Hypotheses on the origin of its trademark pattern include the tughra seal of Turkey, the boteh cypress tree that represents death in Zoroastrianism, half of a T'ai Chi symbol, a mango tree, or the leaf of the bodhi tree. When Kashmir fleece was imported from Britain to the Scottish town of this name, weavers spread its eponymous pattern across the world in woolen shawls. Name this comma-shaped design adapted from Mughal artwork and still found on ties and other clothing.

His religious works include Pharoah and His Host Lost in the Red Sea and Christ Healing the Sick. This painter of Agrippina Landing at Brundisium used distinctive large, almond-shaped eyes in his portraits. Though American-born, he helped found the Royal Academy before painting Death on the Pale Horse and Penn's Treaty with the Indians. Name this painter who sparked a controversy by using contemporary figures in classical poses for his depiction of the taking of Quebec in The Death of General Wolfe.

This term can be used for work as diverse as that of Otto Wagner and Joseph Olbrich, who opposed Wagner's classicism and formed the Vienna Secession. It is exemplified by Victor Horta's Hotel Tassel, inspired by the works of Charles Rennie Macintosh. Architect Hector Guimard used it for the Paris Metro signs, and it also popped up as Spain's "modernisme" and Germany's Jugendstil (YOO gind shteel). Name this movement also practiced by Antonio Gaudi and shown at the Universal Exposition of 1900, exemplified by the painting of Gustav Klimt and the glassmaking of Louis Tiffany.

His classically inspired sculptures include The Rape of Proserpina and Apollo and Daphne, which were executed for Cardinal Borghese. More extravagant works include a baldacchino over the high altar in St. Peter's Basilica and the Fountain of the Four Rivers. His masterpiece sits under a hidden window in the Cornaro Chapel, and shows an angel driving an arrow into the heart of a female mystic. Name this Italian Baroque sculptor of The Ecstasy of St. Teresa.

Igor Stravinsky and Paul Hindemith contributed commissions for the fiftieth anniversary of this organization founded by Henry Lee Higginson, while Sergei Rachmaninov refused its conductorship on several different occasions. It is the orchestra-in-residence at the Tanglewood Music Festival each summer, and it has been conducted by Arthur Nikisch, Charles Munch (moonk), and Serge Koussevitsky. In 2004, James Levine replaced Seiji Ozawa as principal conductor of, what orchestra whose regular home is Symphony Hall in the Back Bay Fens?

The son of Matthew Arnold, a dog swimming in the Wye, and quotes from Mendelssohn's "Calm Sea and Prosperous Voyage" appear in sections ranging from "C.A.E." to "E.D.U." Its most analyzed passage represents a discussion about the slow movements of Beethoven. Its principal melody is allegedly a counterpoint to "Auld Lang Syne" or "Rule Britannia," and the noted ninth section is a portrait of A. J. Jaeger entitled "Nimrod." fourteen people and a dog are "my friends pictured within" what work of Edward Elgar?

They were written while their composer was staying with Johann Peter Salomon following the death of his patron, Prince Nikolaus. Numbered 93 through 104 in the Hoboken catalog, the half of them that are named include the "Clock" and "Drumroll." Written from 1791 to 1795, they also include the "Military," "Miracle," and "Surprise." identify these works written on a foreign excursion from the Esterhazy court by Franz Haydn.

While the Roman cavalry used trumpets, the infantry used this instrument for the same purposes. The Bulgarian gaida and the East European dudy are equivalents that incorporate cowbells, while France's cornemuse is the traditional accompaniment of the hurdy-gurdy or the bombarde at Christmas. The archetypical classical kind, the "piobroch," was created by Iain Odhar and the MacCrimmon family. Name this musical instrument whose distinguished sound is produced by the contrast of a chanter and several drones, similar to the Irish "union pipe" but originating in Scotland.

Often omitted from reproductions of the painting are the three lunettes containing the coat-of-arms of the Sforza family, which commissioned it. A doorway was cut into it in 1656, as by that time the work was unrecognizable. The most extensive reconstruction effort on it was spearheaded by Pinin Barcilon [bahr shee LOHN] between 1978 and 1999 at its home in the convent of Santa Maria della Grazie in Milan. A Maundy Thursday meeting of thirteen people is depicted in what painting by Leonardo da Vinci?

On the left, a bearded man hangs his feet over the foam-covered water as he stirs his oar, while another man just in front him faces the viewer as he paddles his own oar. Several boats can be seen in the background on the right, as can a man in green who faces the center as he steers. The dominant image is an American flag, positioned upright in the center of the boat, behind the title character, clad in a general's uniform and standing on one knee at the edge of the boat. Name this Emmanuel Leutze painting of the future first president and his men rowing towards Trenton.

Among twentieth century composers, the foremost sets in this genre are Béla Bartók's six and Dmitri Shostakovich's fifteen. Arnold Schoenberg's second unusually requires a soprano soloist, while a movement of Samuel Barber's first was later re-orchestrated as his Adagio. Luigi Boccherini wrote ninety-one of them; Schubert wrote fifteen, including Death and the Maiden and Rosamunde; and Beethoven's fifteen include the Grosse Fuge. Identify this musical genre written for cello, viola, and first and second violins.

A popular anecdote tells how this painting's artist was heavily distracted by two swans as he painted its background while on the banks of the Hogsmill River. Another story describes how Elizabeth Siddall, the model for the title character, caught a cold after posing in a bathtub for hours. Flowers and plants are portrayed in painstaking detail in this Pre-Raphaelite work, including the necklace of violets around the titular literary character as she lies drowning in the river. Name this John Millais painting of a female character from Hamlet.

Previous recordings omitted a prominent percussion instrument or replaced it with an attacca on the drum. For several years in its composer's home country, Mikhail Glinka's "Glory" replaced "God Save the Tsar" at the end of this work, although La Marseillaise remained in this depiction of the victory at Borodino. Name this piece scored for orchestra and a cannon, by Pyotr Tschaicovsky.

Popular arias in this opera include the soprano "Caro nome," sung by a lovestruck Gilda before she is kidnapped by courtiers, and the tenor arias "Questa o quella" and "La donna è mobile," both of which celebrate the romantic flings of the Duke of Mantua. The plot is driven by a curse Monterone invokes upon the title character, whose daughter Gilda dies at the hands of the assassin Sparafucile. Identify this Verdi opera about the tragedies that befall a court jester.

Ernst Barlach was one of the few sculptors to work in this style. Its precursors go back to Matthias Grünewald, but it took its modern impetus from Gauguin's exclusion of shadows and use of folk methods, and the unique color and line stylizations of Van Gogh. For 10 points—name this art movement which abandoned Impressionism's goal of painting that which is seen in favor of representing emotion.

A sixteenth-century organist and composer of The King's Hunt inspired a character in John Arbuthnot's Law is a Bottomless Pit, who in turn lent his name and personality to this cultural icon. His traditional outfit is "a squat top hat, neckcloth, tailcoat, tight breeches," boots, and a waistcoat adorned with a flag. _FOR TEN POINTS_, name this personification of England, analogous to the United States' Uncle Sam.

When Michelangelo heard that this contemporary and his workshop had completed a massive commission in less than one hundred days, the master snidely remarked, "So it seems." A major proponent of the Mannerist style, he painted over Leonardo's deteriorating fresco of the Battle of Anghiari and produced many other works for his patron, Duke Cosimo I in Florence. FOR TEN POINTS—name this sixteenth-century Italian, author of the two-volume biography of artists, Lives.

He committed suicide shortly after finishing 14 large paintings for the de Menil family. His early work stressed such themes as the loneliness of human beings in urban scenes such as his "Subway" series. Influenced by the theories of Carl Jung, this painter sought to elicit moods through the use of color. Name this abstract expressionist, known for using soft-edged rectangles of color.

In his work, this composer formulated the "21 note scale" designed to "drown" the sense of tonality, though this system was never adhered to in the inflexible manner of Schoenberg's 12-tone system. In 1873, he entered the Paris Conservatory, and eventually won the Grand Prix de Rome with his cantata L'Enfant Prodigue. _FOR 10 POINTS_\--name this French composer better known for Suite Bergamesque, La Mer, and Prelude to the Afternoon of a Faun.

With Charles Eames, he designed a unique chair which won first prize in a competition at the Museum of Modern Art in 1940. He is better known for architecture, for such works as the curved forms of Dulles Airport and the TWA Terminal at Kennedy International Airport. Name this man, best known for his Jefferson Memorial Arch in St. Louis.

In his Portrait of Emile Zola, he added in the background Kuniaki's portrait of a sumo wrestler, indicative of his interest in Japanese art. He finally succumbed to the persuasion of his future sister-in-law Berthe Morisot [more-ee-soh] that he began to paint outdoors like the Impressionists, whose exhibitions he did not participate in. _FOR 10 POINTS_\--name this artist whose works include Olympia and The Bar at the Folies-Bergere.

They can be closed, semi-closed, semi-open, or open in manner of articulation; front, central, or back in place of articulation; rounded or unrounded; voiced or unvoiced. They are defined as phonemes, which are pronounced with an unobstructed vocal tract, and they can be melded into diphthongs or triphthongs. Identify these sounds which, in English, include e and I.

Erich Korngold's is cast in a single movement, while Ned Rorem's [roar em] is in eight movements. Both Britten and Richard Strauss were asked to write them, but nothing became of those requests. Prokofiev's variant, his fourth, was still rejected by Paul Wittgenstein, the soloist who commissioned it, noting that he "didn't understand a note of it." FTP, name this classical genre, the most famous work of which was composed by Maurice Ravel at the same time as his Piano Concerto in G major.
Piano concerto for the left hand

On a stepladder in the lower right of this work is one man and a woman in red. Another woman holds the central figure's foot. Two men are climbing on the title object; one has a mouth full of cloth and is grasping the arm of the central figure. Identify this painting in which a corpse is being removed from a torture device, the central panel of the Antwerp triptych by Peter Paul Rubens.

He studied the work of Giovanni Palestrina after winning the 1839 Prix de Rome, but he drew inspiration from another past composer for one of his most- performed sacred works. Recently coming into popularity is his opera La Colombe, while his other operas include Polyeucte, Sappho, Philémon et Baucis, and the 1867 Roméo et Juliette. _FOR 10 POINTS—_ name this composer of a variation on a Bach melody entitled Ave Maria as well as the Funeral March of a Marionette and the 1859 opera Faust.

While the title characters hunt, a Sorceress plots against them. She sends a witch, who tells the male title character he must leave his wife, and found a new city. When he obeys the false god's command, his jilted wife dies, while the choir sings the funeral dirge "With drooping wings." Noted for its extraordinary "storm" scenes—_ FOR 10 POINTS—_ name this early opera by Henry Purcell.

Along with evening classes at the School of Fine Arts, he took painting lessons from Swiss painter Charles Gleyre. There he was soon joined by Claude Monet, Alfred Sisley, and Frederic Bazille; where he befriended and painted portraits of all three. His early work, such as "The Theatre Box," was Impressionistic, but subsequent trips to Provence, Italy, and Algeria made in 1881 and 1882 turned him toward painting in neoclassical style of Ingres but with more color, as in "The Umbrellas." _FOR TEN POINTS_—identify this French painter, perhaps best known for his "Bathers" series.

One artist from this country depicted scenes such as "Modern Human Sacrifice" and "Gods of the Modern World" in his work The Epic of American Civilization. Another artist from this country controversially depicted Lenin in a work that was later redone as Man, Controller of the Universe. Self- portraits by one artist from this country include one in which two versions of her are connected by an artery, and another with a monkey on her shoulder. Name this country, home to the muralists Jose Orozco and Diego Rivera, as well as Frida Kahlo.

Leos Janacek wrote one of these works based off a glagolitic text. Haydn wrote one of this type of work in D minor that was attended by and nicknamed after Admiral Lord Nelson. Another of this type of work by Palestrina was named after Pope Marcellus. A famous example of this type of composition written by Johann Sebastian Bach and is in B minor. Works of this type contain sections including a Kyrie, Sanctus, and Agnus Dei. Name this type of choral composition, which sets the liturgy to music.

This city's tallest building, completed in 2001, is the 974-foot Comcast Center, and Lancaster Avenue runs through this city's "Main Line", including its suburbs of Wayne and Bryn Mawr. Universities in this city lying along the Delaware and Schuylkill (SKOO-kull) Rivers include Drexel, Temple, and the University of Pennsylvania. Name this fifth-largest city in the United States, the "city of brotherly love" and cheesesteaks which is home to Independence Hall and the Liberty Bell.

Fall Kickoff Tournament Written by the OSU Academic Team Extras/Tiebreakers One painting by this artist shows a man resting his hand on the sculpted head of a Greek playwright. Another painting by this artist depicts the writing on the wall in very bright light. In addition to painting Aristotle Contemplating a Bust of Homer and Belshazzar's Feast, this painter created a work depicting the dissection of an arm. In another painting, this artist showed a small girl amongst a group of soldiers led by Frans Banning Cocq. Name this Dutch painter of The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp and The Night Watch.

This artist depicted lazing Venetian oarsmen in his Gondolier's Siesta. In another painting by this man, soldiers with bandages around their eyes grab onto their comrades soldiers as they march in-line between rows of the dead, and this creator of the massive anti-war Gassed showed a lighter touch when painting a scene in which two young girls in white gowns play with paper lanterns surrounded by the titular flowers in his Carnation, Lily, Lily, Rose. The premier of this man's portrait of a black-gowned Virginie Amelie Gautreau was a disappointment, as it was received as scandalous for the time. Name this artist of Madame X.

The third act of this composer's oratorio Solomon begins with the orchestra playing the "Arrival of the Queen of Sheba." This composer wrote several coronation anthems for George II, which included "Zadok the Priest." "La Rejouissance" is a movement in a work by this man that celebrates the end of a war. Another orchestral work by this composer includes the "Alla Hornpipe" and was likely written for river festivities. Name the composer of Music for the Royal Fireworks and Water Music, who included the "Hallelujah Chorus" in his Messiah.

On this painting's right side, an orange grove lies on the edge of the open water. A nymph on the right waits to drape the main subject in a pink cloak covered in flora designs, symbolic of fertility. The central figure's orange hair, tied together in a light blue ribbon gently blows out of her face as two figures, Zephyrus and Chloris, blow her to shore. Name this fifteenth century painting of the Roman goddess of love emerging from the sea on a scallop shell, a work by Botticelli.

This composer included "Va, pensiero," also known as the Chorus of the Hebrew Slaves, in first major opera Nabucco. Another of this composer's operas describes Di Luna's persecution of Manrico and contains the "Anvil Chorus." This composer also wrote an opera that features the aria "La donna e mobile." This Italian composer of Il Trovatore is also known for a work in which the title Ethiopian princess joins her lover Radames in getting buried alive. Name this 19th century composer, best known for such operas such as Rigoletto and Aida.

A woman hold out her arms to reach a baby holding the head of a lamb in this artist's The Virgin and Child with St. Anne. Two paintings of the same name by this man show Mary holding her hand over the head of an infant Jesus. This artist of Madonna of the Rocks created a fresco in which the Twelve Disciples are grouped into threes, and Judas can be seen holding a bag of silver. In addition to painting The Last Supper, this artist painted a portrait of a woman that contains an enigmatic smile. Name the Renaissance artist of the Mona Lisa.

One of this composer's virtuosic pieces is a work for solo cello titled Rococo Variations. His fourth symphony has a movement where the strings play entirely in pizzicato, and is followed by his Manfred Symphony. Though not a member of The Five, one of this composer's works was commissioned to commemorate Russia successfully rebuffing an invasion by Napoleon and includes cannon fire as part of the score. Name this Russian composer of the 1812 Overture as well as the ballets Swan Lake and The Nutcracker.

One player of this instrument included environmental messages in his album Global Warming. That player is Sonny Rollins, who plays the tenor type of this instrument. Another jazzist who played this instrument wrote pieces such as "Ornithology," whose names were based on his nicknamed of "Yardbird." A performer of this instrument was the creator of the albums Giant Steps and A Love Supreme. Charlie Parker and John Coltrane played what instrument, which is often associated with jazz and has an alto type?

One painting by this artist depicts a restaurant with a green ceiling and five customers hunched over tables. Among this artist's final works is his Wheatfield with Crows. Paintings such as The Yellow House were painted while this artist resided in Arles, during which he spent time with Paul Gauguin. This artist's still lifes include several depictions of sunflowers, and his later self-portraits show him with a bandaged ear. Name the Dutch post-Impressionist who painted The Night Cafe and Starry Night.

Composers who wrote studies for this instrument include Carl Czerny and Muzio Clementi. The only piece in Carnival of the Animals not describing animals instead depicts two people playing scales on this instrument. John Cage inserted various objects to produce the "prepared" type of this instrument. Four concertos were written for this instrument by Sergei Rachmaninoff. Among the many works for this instrument by Frederic Chopin are his Funeral March and "Black Key" Etude. Name this keyboard instrument with 88 keys.

This sculptor's works include a plate known as the Chellini Madonna and a wooden statue of Mary Magdalene. One of this man's equestrian statues depicts Erasmo di Narni. In addition to the Gattamelata, this man created several works for the Orsanmichele, including his statue of St. Mark. In this man's most famous sculpture, a naked youth wearing only a laurel hat and boots puts his foot over the decapitated head of Goliath. Name the Italian Renaissance sculptor of the bronze David.

This composer described "Night Moths" and "Sad Birds" in a work for piano, Miroirs. This composer's Piano Concerto in G major opens with the sound of a whiplash, and his other piano concerto was written for the left hand. The poems of Aloysius Bertrand were the inspiration for his Gaspard de la Nuit. The composer's most famous work began with a commission by Ida Rubinstein, and maintains a steady crescendo and snare drum ostinato rhythm though the entire piece. Name the composer of Bolero.

In this opera's first act, a group of boys mimics the changing of the guard. The protagonist of this opera is asked by his mother to marry the virtuous Micaela, but is tossed a flower by another woman. The title character escapes arrest after singing the Seguidilla in this opera, which follows an aria describing love as a rebellious bird, the "Habanera." This opera also includes the Toreador Song, which is sung by Escamillo. Name this opera about Don Jose's relationship with the title gypsy, an opera by Georges Bizet.

This composer's Symphony No. 4 in E minor contains a chaconne, while his first symphony was dubbed "Beethoven's Tenth" by critic Hans von Bulow.. This composer wrote the Tragic Overture as a companion piece to a work that contains drinking songs and was written to celebrate his degree from the University of Breslau, the Academic Festival Overture. Another of this composer's works uses text from the Lutheran Bible. Name the composer of A German Requiem who also wrote a famous lullaby.

One painting by this artist shows two women in yellow dress and blue bonnets attending a meeting of various composers. That painting was Music in the Tuileries. A painting by this man shows a black servant holding flowers next to a prostitute lying on a white bed, and that painting caused a scandal when presented to the Salon. Another controversial painting by this artist shows two high class men at a picnic with a nude woman. Name this French artist of Olympia and Luncheon on the Grass.

Dmitri Shostakovich's eighth work of this type contains his DSCH motif. Bedrich Smetana wrote two of this type of work, the first of which includes a polka and is subtitled "From My Life." Borodin's second composition of this type contains a famous Nocturne. The so-called "Father" of this type of composition wrote them in collections such as "Sun" and "Erdody." name this type of musical composition pioneered by Franz Joseph Haydn, which is played by an ensemble of two violins, a viola, and a cello.

This city's recently completed buildings includes the Frank Gehry-designed 8 Spruce Street and examples of modernist architecture in this city include the TWA Flight center. The Four Seasons Restaurant in this city can be found in a skyscraper built in the International style, the Seagram Building. Buildings in this city that have held the title of world's tallest include the Woolworth Building and the Chrysler Building. Name this city, home to the One World Trade Center and the Empire State Building.

In one work by this artist, three women stand smugly in front of a picture of Washington Crossing the Delaware. That 1932 painting is a satire of the elitist attitude displayed by that group, Daughters of Revolution. In his most famous work, a red barn stands in the background behind the right shoulder of a man holding a pitchfork. Name this American regionalist painter, known for his 1930 portrait of an Iowa farm couple, American Gothic.

This composer wrote a ballet in which the title character obtains a golden mask after descending to Hades to retrieve his wife Eurydice. That ballet, Orpheus, was written during this composer's neo-Classical period, during which he also produced the Dumbarton Oaks Concerto. Prince Ivan defeats the evil Kastchei with the help of the title avian in another of this composer's ballets, while his most famous ballet depicted "Scenes from Pagan Russia" and sparked a riot at its premiere in Paris. Name the composer of The Firebird and The Rite of Spring.

This twentieth-century composer's ballets include Romeo and Juliet and Cinderella. He became prominent with the Scythian Suite for piano and his first symphony, nicknamed the "Classical." While The Fiery Angel may be his greatest opera, War and Peace is his most ambitious. For 10 points—name this Russian composer of Love for Three Oranges.

His dramatic works include the ballet The Victory of Love and Ulysses's Return to his Homeland. His choral music includes nine books of madrigals and the Vespers of the Blessed Virgin. His studies under Jacopo Peri inspired his work, some of the earliest of the baroque period, including The Coronation of Poppea. For 10 points—name this Italian who, in 1607, composed Orfeo, the earliest significant opera.

In the background, two men and a woman walk up a dark stairway to avoid seeing what is about to transpire. In the midground, a man rests his arms and head on the wall. In the foreground, a shirtless man raises a hand to the skies, while a distraught man in red stares at the ground as he passes a potent goblet to the contemplative central figure. For 10 points—name this 1787 depiction of a forced suicide by Jacques-Louis David.

His initial work as a painter in a porcelain factory helped him gain experience with light, fresh colors that distinguished his work as an Impressionist. His 1869 La Grenouillière is considered a classic early statement of the Impressionistic style, but by 1882, he felt he needed a greater sense of solidarity in his work, as seen in The Umbrellas. For 10 points—name this French painter of The Luncheon of the Boating Party.

One wing of the enemy's helmet remains stiff and metallic, while the other reaches up to caress the leg of the hero. The hero wears nothing but a pair of boots and a hat crowned with laurel and has shoulder-length hair. Holding the sword of his vanquished foe, the title subject stands with one foot on the cheek of his enemy. For 10 points—name this bronze sculpture by Donatello in which a Biblical hero rests after killing Goliath.

Its earliest printed version of the tune can be found in a 1775 volume of airs. Henri Vieuxtemps based his Caprice burlesque on it, Anton Rubenstein wrote variations on it, and Antonin Dvorak included it in the finale of the New World symphony. For 10 points—name this tune concerning an American who went to town riding on a pony.

Originally developed by merchants to express frustrations at being socially inferior despite economic success. Its principal themes are conflicts between humanity and the feudal system, in such plays as The House of Suguwara. For 10 points—name this form of drama in which men called onnagata play the female parts.
